feedback: If a child answers 'how many altogether' with the number of categories (e.g. 4 kinds of pet), return to the data and add the category counts, then check the sum equals the number of children surveyed.

If a child reads a neighbouring category's count or is off by one, steady the reading: track the row across to its count with a finger or ruler. This is a reading lapse to steady, not a concept to reteach.
Prompt 'how did you work out how many more?' to check a difference was computed rather than a value read.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a single value, totalling all values, and comparing two values are three different moves; the total must reconcile with the whole group, and a comparison asks for a gap between two values.
learnerActions: Collect a small survey (e.g. favourite pet) from your class or family and build it into a pictogram or block diagram.
Answer single-category questions first: 'How many children chose rabbits?' by reading the one row/column.
Answer a total question: 'How many children are there altogether?' by summing ALL the category frequencies, not counting how many kinds of pet there are.
Check your total against the number of people actually surveyed as a self-check.
Answer a comparison question: 'How many more chose dogs than cats?' by finding the difference.
Each time you give a comparison answer, say out loud how you got it.
activities.title: Question ladder on your own pets chart

feedback: If a child gives the taller category's count (8) as the comparison answer, line the two categories up one-to-one, count the unmatched part, and name that 'how many more' means the gap/difference, then re-ask.
To test the comparison on a small gap, ask 'which two categories are closest — how many more does one have than the other?'
A bar model or number line can make the subtraction visible for the 'how many more' step.
activities.intendedInsight: 'How many more' is the gap between the two categories — the unmatched part — not the height or count of the bigger one.
learnerActions: Pick two categories to compare, e.g. dogs and cats.
Line the two rows up one-to-one so matching items sit directly beside each other.
Count the unmatched part that sticks out on the taller row — that is 'how many more'.
Confirm the same answer by subtracting: taller count minus shorter count (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3).
Say the result in comparison words: 'There are 3 more dogs than cats' and 'there are 3 fewer cats than dogs.'
activities.title: Line them up to see the difference

feedback: If the combined total or grand total doesn't match the group, return to the organised data, re-add the category counts, and locate the misread or miscount.
Ask the child to state, in their own words, why the category totals must add up to the whole group.
activities.intendedInsight: Categories can be combined by adding their counts, and the sum of all categories should reconcile with the whole surveyed group — a built-in check on your reading.
learnerActions: Answer 'if the rabbit and cat groups joined, how many would that be?' by adding the two category counts.
Answer 'does your total match how many people you actually surveyed?' and, if not, recount.
Explain why, when each person surveyed gave exactly one answer, the total of all categories should equal the number of people surveyed.
activities.title: Combine and reconcile checks
